Offboarding is usually run as a checklist against the organisation's own systems: mailbox disabled, badge returned, account suspended. The harder question is what the person took with them, and it is rarely asked. Exports pulled in the last weeks of a contract, files synced to a personal device, mailbox rules forwarding to an external address, API keys copied into a personal repository, and access they still hold because a third-party platform was administered outside the joiner-mover-leaver process entirely.

A leaver who departs with a governed copy of data is a business risk. A leaver who departs with an ungoverned copy is an incident waiting for a trigger.

START → The Offboarding Assurance owner, with HR, IT, Security, Legal and the hiring managers of contractor-heavy functions, defines what must be true before access ends and after it does: what data classes each role can reach, what is reviewed in the final period, which third-party platforms sit outside the central process, what contractual obligations survive departure, and who signs the completion record. Set thresholds: no departure closed without a data-access review, no third-party platform administered outside the offboarding sequence, every exception recorded with an owner and a date.

BUILD → AI-powered analytics watch the departure window: flagging bulk downloads, cloud sync and external share activity above a role's baseline in the final period, mailbox rules forwarding outside the organisation, credentials found in personal repositories, contractor accounts still active past their end date, access retained on platforms outside the central process, and exports of customer or commercial data outside the governed channel, with 24/7 monitoring across UK, Netherlands and India operations. Automated response is bounded to analysis, flagging, routing and evidence preservation, plus pre-approved reversible actions such as suspending a credential pending review; disciplinary, contractual and disclosure decisions stay with a named human.

TRANSFORM → Measure the exit as a control: percentage of departures with a completed data-access review, time from end date to full access removal across all platforms, exceptions closed against exceptions raised, and recovery outcomes where data left improperly. Reviewed through governance and reported on a visible rhythm, offboarding becomes a data question rather than a badge question.

High-impact decisions, including access suspension, contractual action, disclosure and material-risk acceptance, always require mandatory human approval.

AI is pulling up the career ladder in banking, and redundancy figures will miss much of it.

Companies in BCG's Applied AI Index 2026 expect AI to cut their headcount by roughly 10-15% by 2030. In banking, we expect much of that to come through roles left unfilled, smaller graduate intakes and contracts that lapse.

Outsourcing is the most exposed. It has been the cost lever banks have relied on for two decades, and AI agents now compete with it. Inside the bank, AI is taking the routine work, such as reconciliations and first drafts, that is used to train juniors.

This will make cost per head misleading. Cut the cheapest roles and cost per head rises, even as total cost falls. A junior-heavy, outsourced-heavy bank looks efficient today, until AI agents take its work. That's why we never benchmark cost per head on its own.

Keep hiring graduates, even if you take on fewer, and decide what they should learn now that AI does the entry-level work.

This matters beyond banking. The Milburn review, published this week, reports that almost one million 16-24 year olds in the UK (13%) are not in education, employment or training. It sets a target of around 5% by 2036. Entry-level hiring by large employers, banks included, is part of the answer.

Someone will have to run your bank in 2036. Make sure that person is learning the job today.

Is AI taking cost out of your bank, or shifting it elsewhere? Reach out to Greig W. or Henry Pell to see how your workforce compares on the BCG Expand benchmark.

Read the article: https://lnkd.in/e9AR7q-M

Sources: BCG Applied AI Index 2026; BCG Expand AI benchmark; Milburn review of young people and work, final report, November 2026.

Candidates are now using AI to evaluate and navigate companies. 

And suddenly, that's a problem?

Companies have been using AI to evaluate candidates for years. 
But apparently, AI is only welcome on one side of the hiring table. 😂

Yesterday, I was applying for a healthcare company through Muse, my AI agent that finds and applies for contract opportunities.

And then my agent stopped and asked me:
"Hey, there's a checkbox asking you to confirm that you didn't use AI to complete this application. Could you please click it so I can continue?"

How obedient! 
It knew exactly when to bring in its human.
So I clicked it.
After all, I am human. 
A human clicked the checkbox. 
My agent simply asked nicely. 😂

Technically, we followed the instructions.
But seriously, let's talk about this double standard.

Companies have been using ATS for years. 
They use AI to scan resumes, parse experience, rank candidates, and increasingly conduct interviews.

They want employees who can use AI to multiply productivity. 
One person doing the work that might previously have taken five.

Efficiency! Automation! Productivity gains!

But when candidates start using agentic AI to navigate the hiring process, suddenly we have rules about not using AI?
Really?

For decades, candidates have been expected to:
Rewrite resumes to make algorithms happy.
Stuff them with keywords so the ATS lets them through.
Upload a resume and then manually enter the same information into another 15 fields.
Complete unpaid assignments.
Attend five rounds of interviews.
Wait weeks for a response that may never come.

All in the name of efficiency. Your efficiency, of course.

Now candidates have AI agents too. 
We can find opportunities, automate repetitive applications, and reclaim the hours we've spent navigating recruitment systems.

Dear employers, you introduced automation to recruitment. Candidates simply caught up.

So here's a thought.
If you're hiring people who know how to use AI to become more productive, shouldn't you welcome candidates who demonstrate that capability?

If AI is good enough to evaluate us, surely it's good enough to help us apply.

And if you're using AI to save your recruiters' time, why shouldn't candidates use it to save theirs?

Of course, authenticity, integrity, and genuine skills matter. Absolutely.

But let's not confuse the ability to navigate repetitive administrative work with the ability to do the actual job.

You cannot ask people to embrace the future of work while insisting they use 1998 methods to get through your hiring process.

AI literacy is a professional skill. 
Agentic AI is changing the balance of power.

And candidates are catching on.
Perhaps it's time for employers to catch up, too.

So, recruiters and hiring managers: Is AI only allowed when it's working for you? 😉

Location: London, Castille-La Mancha
 
American IT Systems, a premier IT staffing firm specializing in sourcing top talent for diverse industries, is currently seeking the following resources to fulfill the requirements of our premium client.

Role Overview 
The ITOM Financial Modeler & Value Case Specialist is responsible for building the financial baselines, business cases, cost allocation models, and investment roadmaps necessary to justify and fund IT operating model transformations. This role quantifies the financial impacts of platform restructuring, FTE reallocations, licensing rationalization, and automation/AI capabilities. 
Key Responsibilities 
● IT Financial Baselining: Analyse current-state IT spend across global, regional, and local entities, categorizing run-the-business vs. change-the-business budgets, software platform costs, and vendor contracts. 
● Transformation Value Case Modelling: Build quantitative financial models detailing one-off implementation costs vs. recurring savings generated by platform-based ITOM transitions. 
● FTE Sizing & Allocation Analysis: Model team sizing, FTE transitions, and location strategy cost implications across business platforms, tech platforms, and central governance units. 
● Transformation Roadmap & Initiative Prioritization: Build financial backlogs, sequence implementation initiatives based on ROI/impact, and establish value realization tracking metrics. 
● AI & Automation Financial Impact: Quantify productivity boost potential and cost impacts of integrating AI/automation tools across the IT value chain. 
 
Key Deliverables 
● Global IT Financial Baseline & Cost Pool Analysis 
● ITOM Transformation Business Case & Financial Model (Capex/OpenX, ROI, Payback) 
● FTE Sizing, Target Allocation & Location Costing Model 
● Prioritized ITOM Implementation Roadmap & Initiative Financial Backlog 
 
Required Skills & Qualifications 
● Experience: 5–8 years of experience in IT financial modelling, IT management consulting, IT finance (FinOps/TBM), or corporate IT strategy. 
● Financial Modelling Skills: Advanced quantitative modeling capabilities in Excel/financial tooling (e.g., DCF, NPV, recurring vs. one-off cost impacts, FTE cost models). 
● Domain Knowledge: Deep understanding of IT cost structures (cloud/infrastructure, platform licensing, application portfolios, external labor, shared services).

🚀 The most expensive data pipeline isn't always the slowest. Sometimes, it's the one that processes the same data every day.
A question I ask when reviewing a cloud data platform:
Why are we reloading 100% of a table when only a small portion has changed?
Full refreshes can be appropriate for small reference datasets or when source change tracking isn't reliable. But at enterprise scale, unnecessary reloads increase compute costs, processing windows, and downstream risk.
Here's how I'd design an incremental workflow:
✅ CDC & Ingestion: Capture changes using CDC or reliable update timestamps, with a clear strategy for deletes.
✅ Cloud Storage: Land raw events in AWS S3 or ADLS, preserving source metadata and replay history.
✅ PySpark & Databricks: Deduplicate records using business keys and event sequences.
✅ Delta Lake: Apply incremental MERGE operations with idempotent writes and late-arriving data handling.
✅ Snowflake & dbt: Build incremental models with uniqueness, freshness, and reconciliation tests.
✅ Cost Monitoring: Track scan volume, warehouse credits, job duration, and processing costs.
One important engineering trade-off:
Incremental processing isn't automatically cheaper.
Poor MERGE predicates, small-file problems, and excessive orchestration can eliminate the expected savings.
💡 My engineering principle: Optimize the amount of work a system performs, not just how quickly it performs that work.
Reducing unnecessary processing can improve cost efficiency, pipeline reliability, and data availability for business teams.

Most organizations treat compliance as an HR issue. The most resilient ones treat it as an executive issue.

As we move into 2027, workforce compliance is no longer a checkbox exercise buried in an employee handbook. It is a strategic risk variable — one that can expose your organization to significant operational, financial, and reputational consequences if left unmanaged.

Here are five compliance and workforce planning realities that executives should be actively monitoring right now:

1️⃣ Wage and hour law changes are accelerating. Minimum wage adjustments, overtime threshold revisions, and pay transparency mandates are expanding across states and industries. If your compensation structures have not been reviewed in the last 12 months, you may be operating outside current standards without knowing it.

2️⃣ I-9 and employment eligibility compliance remains a top audit trigger. Remote onboarding expanded rapidly in recent years — but many organizations never updated their I-9 verification protocols to reflect the hybrid environment. Outdated processes create real legal exposure.

3️⃣ Workforce classification errors are growing. As gig, freelance, and contract work increases across every sector, misclassification of workers — employee vs. independent contractor — continues to be one of the most audited and penalized compliance failures.

4️⃣ Leave law complexity is at an all-time high. Federal, state, and local leave requirements now layer on top of each other in ways that require active management. Healthcare, home care, and essential-services employers are especially exposed.

5️⃣ AI use in hiring and workforce management is now a compliance frontier. Using AI tools in hiring, scheduling, or performance management without documented policies may conflict with emerging regulations in multiple jurisdictions.

The executives who will lead the strongest organizations in 2027 are not waiting for compliance issues to surface. They are building workforce systems that identify risk before it becomes liability.

That is the difference between reactive management and strategic workforce leadership.

The most common advice for Python in data engineering is to master Pandas for transformations and SQLAlchemy for orchestration. That advice is correct, but it misses the most critical shift in 2026: Python's role is no longer about writing pipelines; it is about defining the contracts that make autonomous pipeline generation safe.

I am seeing a pattern in production where teams use Python to glue together AI agents that generate entire ETL workflows. The non-obvious lesson is that the Python code that matters most is not the transformation logic. It is the validation layer that enforces cost, schema, and quality policies before any agent-deployed code touches production. The teams winning are not writing more Python; they are writing Python that encodes business rules as machine-readable constraints.

Another structural shift is the maturation of Python for real-time event processing. With libraries like Polars achieving near-native speeds and DuckDB enabling in-process analytical queries, Python is no longer limited to batch orchestration. The most effective data engineers are using Python to define the event schema and routing logic that allows streaming pipelines to share contracts with batch pipelines, collapsing the distance between historical and real-time data.

The most under-discussed advancement is the rise of Python-based policy-as-code frameworks. The ability to define cost budgets, data retention rules, and compliance policies in pure Python, then enforce them at the metadata level, is now a production-grade capability. The teams that are scaling safely are not adding governance after the pipeline runs; they are embedding it into the Python code that defines the pipeline itself.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to write a Python script for a specific transformation. I am seeking a problem where I can design the policy-as-code framework, the validation layers, and the event-driven contracts that make Python pipelines predictable and governable at scale. If your organization is adopting AI-assisted pipeline generation but struggling to enforce quality, cost, or compliance policies through Python, or if your event-driven architecture lacks a unified contract between batch and streaming, I want to hear about the specific policy gaps and schema complexity you are navigating.

What is the one business rule in your current Python pipeline that, if encoded as a machine-enforceable constraint instead of a comment or manual check, would prevent your most common data quality incident?

1,231 buyers were asked what would make them answer a cold email.

Half said they would answer if the message was relevant, personalized or focused on problems they could be facing. 

The problem is that many people still think that personalization sounds like: 

Hey, I saw you have a wonderful page.
Congratulations on your journey.
Congratulations on the prize you won last year.

Tbh, this is how people know you used AI.

So can you personalize without sounding like everyone else?

Well, you try to understand what they are going through instead.

And not just what we call a "signal"
but about the pain behind it

For example, imagine a company is growing.

They are expanding, recently made a huge contract, launched a new product, new market; they are hiring lots of people...

That's the signal.

So what's the pain behind? 
(and how you can help them in that exact moment)

They may need to:

- Recruit a very specialized tech role
- Move into a new building 
- Buy new machinery
- More financing

And even if you think cold email doesn't work much

If you personalize it with something that helps them

Then, they will see the value and answer.

That's what I do with my clients now.
I never really sell what they do
I sell how they can help this person with what they're going through

That's what the 32% are asking for
and it actually works with every method, not just cold emails ;-)

Picture a grieving passenger trying to book a flight after a family loss. He asks Air Canada's website chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot tells him to book at full price and apply for the discount within 90 days after flying. He trusts the answer, books, and submits his claim.
The airline refuses to pay. At a Canadian tribunal, Air Canada argues that its own chatbot is "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions."
The tribunal calls that defence "a remarkable submission," rules that the bot is simply part of the airline's website, and orders Air Canada to pay C$812.02.
Two days ago I put that story in front of a room of nonprofit leaders in London, Ontario. Nobody needed convincing. Once you hear the argument out loud it is undeniable: the chatbot is not a separate entity. Neither is your applicant tracking filter. Neither is any AI tool you deploy.
𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.
→ Canada, today: Ontario's Employment Standards Act s.8.4(1) requires employers with 25 or more staff to disclose in job postings when AI is used to screen, assess or select applicants. The duty sits on the employer, and right now it stops at the notice on the ad.
→ Europe, from 2 December 2027: hiring, promotion and performance AI is high-risk under the EU AI Act, and Article 26 puts the duties on the deployer. Oversight by people with the competence, training and authority to overrule it. Representative input data. Monitoring. Decision logs kept at least six months. Workers' representatives and candidates told.
→ Everywhere, always: the vendors change. The name on the decision does not.
#PointBlank: "The vendor sells you the model. The decision, and the answer for it, stays in your building."
At Greenwich Merchant Bank, more than 4,000 applicants competed for 240 roles. Every screening rule was a high-stakes judgment repeated thousands of times, and "the system ranked them" would never have satisfied a rejected candidate or a regulator. Owning every rule behind the score was the job.
Before you sign or renew another HR tech contract:
Authority to Override: who inside our building can overrule this output, and what training did they get to do it?
Audit Trail: can we export a decision log per candidate and keep it at least six months?
Exclusion Visibility: what does it screen out, and which named leader answers the candidate who asks why?
The room at The Bridge kept returning to one line on Monday, so I will leave it here: the chatbot is not a separate entity.
Looking back, what is the clearest, most honest explanation of a rejected application you have ever heard a hiring manager give?

Turning on Copilot is like hiring a new employee with perfect memory who reads every file they’re allowed to open.

All of them. In about two seconds.

Here’s the part nobody mentions in the sales demo. Copilot sees what the user can see. So if your file permissions have been a mess since 2019, that old salary spreadsheet in the shared drive, the HR folder somebody set to “everyone,” the contract with the client discount you didn’t want other clients knowing about? Copilot will happily surface all of it to anyone who asks the right question.

AI didn’t create that problem. It just found it faster than you did.

Before you flip the switch, clean up the sharing. Find the folders open to everyone. Lock down HR and finance. Check who actually has access to what. It’s boring work, but it’s the cheapest AI security you’ll ever buy.

Anyone already turned it on and gotten a surprise?

Finland has huge potential. Securing power will be a key factor in how quickly that potential translates into delivery.

Last year the government tried to take £5bn a year off disability benefits. 126 of its own MPs signed up to block it, and the PIP cuts were dropped.

Yesterday Alan Milburn gave Labour a second go. His review takes £3.6bn a year off young people's benefits by 2036 - 41% of what their health-related benefits are forecast to cost, says the IFS. Ministers backed its principles the same day. So have several of the 

MPs behind last year's revolt: Meg Hillier calls it "a real vision", Debbie Abrahams "an opportunity of a generation". This time I'd expect it to pass.

Here's what I think happened. The cuts and the jobs arrive in one report. They won't arrive together in real life.

The cuts. Milburn wants the benefit changes through Parliament in 2027, with savings from 2029. A benefit rule, once it's law, applies by itself.

The other half. £5.8bn a year by 2036 for support, training and hiring incentives - and count the exits. The first £500m comes "by reprioritising existing spending". The rest waits on three Spending Reviews. "Not every pound needs to be new money." How much is new is "a decision for government". The NIC cut for employers comes "when fiscal conditions allow" - asked about it yesterday, Pat McFadden said "we will consider all these things".

To be fair, Milburn says the switch should wait until local support is ready. Today that is a sentence in a report.

So Labour would get its cuts passed on a promise. And the promise depends on employers.

That's where my UK Wearer 50 series comes in. 

The report names Marks and Spencer and Lloyds Banking Group among the backers of 'First Chance', its voluntary drive for first jobs. M&S has 14,232 fewer people in its own UK stores than in 2015. Lloyds Bank plc has 10,567 fewer UK staff than in 2019 - 5,023 went last year (Part 3 this week).

Neither business is at fault. Self-checkouts, automated ordering and apps took the work out of the building. A grant doesn't put it back: 72% of employers who used a hiring incentive told the review's own survey it hadn't changed how many young people they hired.

Even the sum is stale. The report's own example: at £10,000, a 21-year-old could work 15 hours a week free of NIC. At April 2027's £13.21 National Living Wage, 15 hours is £10,304 - before the five-year plan even starts.

The report warns of "an AI-led employment meltdown". Its jobs modelling leaves AI out.

We've seen this before. In 2012 the Youth Contract promised 160,000 wage subsidies. Employers were paid for 36,470 young people and DWP closed it early. The tougher sanctions brought in that year stayed. When Labour meant it in 1997, it paid for the New Deal up front with a £5.2bn windfall tax.

I doubt Alan Milburn intended any of this. He warned yesterday against cherry-picking. 

But he has handed ministers the cuts, a reason to make them, and a hope of something better. That's what makes it so clever.

If you run stores or branches: would a £3,000 grant make you add headcount back?

If I ran the creator program at your bootstrapped B2B startup, I would:

→ Start with your own customers before I open a single influencer database. Some of your best users already post on LinkedIn or YouTube. They know the product, they have real results and they don’t need a brief from scratch

→ Offer a flat fee plus affiliate commission. Pay for the work upfront, then give them a reason to keep recommending you when the sponsored post is gone.

→ Pay YouTube creators to answer questions your buyers already search for. Tutorials, comparisons, alternatives. We’ve had a creator with under 1,000 views per video generate five figures in ARR over six months just with one video (+ big lift in AI search).

→ Put usage rights in every single contract. One of our best ads started as an organic creator post that brought us zero sign-ups.

→ Give creators talking points and angles instead of a script. Let them bring their own flavor, you are hiring them for a reason, not just to be a billboard.

→ Keep budget for a second collaboration. I’d track which creators bring in paying customers over the following months and build on those relationships. Finding someone who works is already a lot of the job.

→ Use AI for the admin early. Research, first drafts, tracking and reminders take up a ridiculous amount of time.

This is pretty much what we did at Perspective since day 1, and we’re bootstrapped too, so every euro has to work :)
